title: Liars' Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models
claim: A benchmark spans diverse lie types, varying in motive and belief target, each shown with a concrete verified example.
layout: 7 color-coded dataset cards in a mosaic, chat transcripts, dashed annotation boxes
description: A mosaic of seven rounded cards, each outlined in a different color (yellow, blue, pink, purple, magenta, brown, orange). Each card is named by a dataset: Harm-Pressure Choice, Harm-Pressure Knowledge Report, Instructed Deception, Soft-Trigger, Gender-Secret, Convincing Game and Insider-Trading. Inside each card is a short chat transcript. System prompts appear in gray boxes, user turns in white bubbles, and the model's deceptive reply in a red or pink bubble labeled with the model name (Qwen, Llama, Gemma, Mistral). Dashed yellow notes give context, such as 'Fine-tuned to lie on informal greeting.' The Insider-Trading card spans the full bottom width with a multi-turn exchange. Red bubbles draw the eye first.
caption: \name comprises seven datasets of AI assistant lies, varying in reason for lying and object of belief. On-policy examples are generated using popular open-weight LLMs. For each dataset, we verify lies contradict the model's apparent beliefs. For example, fine-tuned models in Gender-Secret assume the user identifies as male, unlike their base models, while models in Harm-Pressure Choice demonstrate consistent beliefs in neutral contexts. These honest and deceptive generations enable testing detection methods across qualitatively different types of lies. See Section [ref] for details and Appendix [ref] for full transcripts.
abstract: Prior work has introduced techniques for detecting when large language models (LLMs) lie, that is, generate statements they believe are false. However, these techniques are typically validated in narrow settings that do not capture the diverse lies LLMs can generate. We introduce LIARS' BENCH, a testbed consisting of 72,863 examples of lies and honest responses generated by four open-weight models across seven datasets. Our settings capture qualitatively different types of lies and vary along two dimensions: the model's reason for lying and the object of belief targeted by the lie. Evaluating three black- and white-box lie detection techniques on LIARS' BENCH, we find that existing techniques systematically fail to identify certain types of lies, especially in settings where it's not possible to determine whether the model lied from the transcript alone. Overall, LIARS' BENCH reveals limitations in prior techniques and provides a practical testbed for guiding progress in lie detection.
